chapter_summary:
Now that we understand how to arrange `ViewGroup`s to structure our UI, it's time to populate those structures with actual interactive elements – the `View` objects. These are the components users see and interact with directly. We'll focus on four of the most fundamental and frequently used UI elements: `TextView`, `Button`, `ImageView`, and `EditText`. Mastering these will give you a solid foundation for building almost any basic Android app screen.

Let's start with the `TextView`. This is arguably the simplest yet most ubiquitous UI element. Its sole purpose is to display text to the user. You've already seen it in the previous chapter. In XML, you define a `TextView` like this:
```xml
<TextView
    android:id="@+id/greetingTextView"
    android:layout_width="wrap_content"
    android:layout_height="wrap_content"
    android:text="Hello, Android!"
    android:textSize="24sp"
    android:textColor="#FF0000"
    android:textStyle="bold|italic"
    android:padding="8dp"/>
```
Here, `android:id` is crucial because it allows you to uniquely identify this `TextView` so you can reference it from your Kotlin code. `android:text` sets the initial text, `android:textSize` controls the font size, `android:textColor` sets the color (using a hex code or a color resource), and `android:textStyle` allows you to make the text bold, italic, or both. `android:padding` adds space inside the view, between its content and its border. A common mistake is hardcoding text directly into the `android:text` attribute. While convenient for quick examples, in real-world apps, you should always use string resources (defined in `res/values/strings.xml`) like `android:text="@string/hello_android"` for easier localization and maintenance.

Next up is the `Button`. Buttons are interactive elements that users tap to trigger an action. They are fundamental for navigation, submitting forms, or initiating any app functionality.
```xml
<Button
    android:id="@+id/submitButton"
    android:layout_width="wrap_content"
    android:layout_height="wrap_content"
    android:text="Submit"
    android:backgroundTint="#6200EE"
    android:textColor="@android:color/white"
    android:layout_marginTop="16dp"/>
```
Similar to `TextView`, a `Button` has `android:id` and `android:text`. You can also customize its appearance using attributes like `android:backgroundTint` for the button's background color and `android:textColor` for the text color. The real power of a `Button` comes when you attach an `OnClickListener` to it in your Kotlin code, which we'll cover in the next chapter.

The `ImageView` is used to display images. These images can come from your app's drawable resources (images you include in your project), from the internet, or from the device's storage. For now, we'll focus on drawable resources.
```xml
<ImageView
    android:id="@+id/profileImageView"
    android:layout_width="120dp"
    android:layout_height="120dp"
    android:src="@drawable/ic_launcher_foreground"
    android:scaleType="centerCrop"
    android:contentDescription="User profile picture"/>
```
The `android:src` attribute points to the image resource. `android:scaleType` is very important: it defines how the image should be scaled or moved to fit the `ImageView`'s dimensions. Common values include `centerCrop` (scales the image uniformly so that both dimensions are equal to or greater than the corresponding dimension of the view, cropping any excess), `fitCenter` (scales the image uniformly so that both dimensions are less than or equal to the corresponding dimension of the view, centering it), and `center` (centers the image in the view without scaling). Always include `android:contentDescription` for accessibility, providing a textual description of the image for users who cannot see it.

Finally, we have `EditText`, which is a specialized `TextView` that allows users to input and edit text. This is crucial for forms, search bars, and any scenario where user input is required.
```xml
<EditText
    android:id="@+id/nameEditText"
    android:layout_width="match_parent"
    android:layout_height="wrap_content"
    android:hint="Enter your name"
    android:inputType="textPersonName"
    android:minLines="1"
    android:maxLines="1"
    android:padding="12dp"/>
```
Key attributes for `EditText` include `android:hint`, which displays a light-gray placeholder text when the field is empty, guiding the user on what to enter. `android:inputType` is extremely important for usability and safety. It specifies the type of input expected (e.g., `textPersonName`, `number`, `textPassword`, `textEmailAddress`). This helps the system provide the appropriate on-screen keyboard for the user. Forgetting to set an appropriate `inputType` is a common mistake that leads to a poor user experience. `minLines` and `maxLines` can control the height of the `EditText` for multi-line input.

Once you've defined your UI elements in XML, you'll need to interact with them in your Kotlin code. The most common way to do this for beginners is using `findViewById`. This method takes the `id` you assigned in XML (e.g., `R.id.greetingTextView`) and returns a reference to that `View` object.
```kotlin
// Inside your Activity or Fragment's onCreate method
class MainActivity : AppCompatActivity() {
    override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)
        setContentView(R.layout.activity_main)

        // Find the TextView by its ID
        val greetingTextView: TextView = findViewById(R.id.greetingTextView)

        // Now you can modify its properties
        greetingTextView.text = "Welcome, User!"
        greetingTextView.setTextColor(ContextCompat.getColor(this, R.color.purple_200))

        // Find the EditText
        val nameEditText: EditText = findViewById(R.id.nameEditText)
        // You can get its text later, for now just demonstrate finding it
    }
}
```
Notice how `findViewById` requires you to specify the type of `View` (e.g., `TextView`) to ensure type safety. Once you have a reference, you can access and modify its properties, such as `text`, `textColor`, `visibility`, and more. While `findViewById` is fundamental, for larger projects, Android developers often use View Binding or Data Binding for more efficient and type-safe access to UI elements, but `findViewById` remains a core concept to understand. Always ensure the `id` you use in `findViewById` exactly matches the `android:id` in your XML, otherwise your app will crash with a `NullPointerException` at runtime.

screens.title: Working with Common UI Elements (Views)
screens.subtitle: TextView, Button, ImageView, EditText — XML attributes and Kotlin access

narration.text: In this lesson we will populate layouts with the four view types you’ll use most: TextView, Button, ImageView, and EditText. You’ll learn which XML attributes control appearance and behavior, how accessibility and input types matter, and how to grab and change views from Kotlin using findViewById. We will also build a small login screen so you can practice placing views with a LinearLayout, configuring ids, hints, input types, and image sources. You will see concrete XML examples for each view and a Kotlin snippet showing how to modify a TextView and read an EditText value. As you follow along, pay attention to common mistakes: hardcoded text instead of string resources, missing ids, and incorrect inputType that leads to the wrong keyboard. Finally, you’ll practice an accessibility habit: always add contentDescription for images. By the end of this chapter you’ll be able to create a simple form, style its basic elements, and connect UI elements to code. Consider how these four views form the backbone of many simple Android screens and what makes each one essential.

keyIdea.title: Core idea
keyIdea.text: Master the four basic view types and learn how XML attributes plus findViewById let you present content and accept input.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Working with Views

In this lesson

Explore key topics
TextView

EditText

Visual overview
T

E

Why this matters
These four elements let you present information, gather user input, and trigger actions. They are the building blocks for forms, settings, and simple app screens.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: In this chapter you’ll learn concrete skills that let you build and control basic Android UI elements. First, you will integrate TextView components into layouts so they display static labels and dynamic content. That skill matters because nearly every app needs readable text and consistent localization practices. Second, you will implement Button components to trigger actions and respond to user taps, and you’ll see how attaching a click listener in Kotlin turns a tap into app behavior. Third, you will utilize ImageView to show drawable resources and understand scaleType and contentDescription for correct display and accessibility. Finally, you will incorporate EditText fields so users can enter names, passwords, or numbers, and you will configure inputType and hints so the keyboard and guidance match the data expected. Each objective includes a small mnemonic or visual cue and a verified competency milestone to track progress. Work through these skills in the hands-on login screen to confirm you can place, configure, and access views programmatically.

narration.text: This second objectives slide focuses on programmatic access and avoiding mistakes. You will practice assigning android:id in XML so Kotlin can find views reliably with findViewById. The lesson will show how to declare types in Kotlin when calling findViewById to keep code type-safe and prevent runtime errors. You will also practice choosing appropriate inputType values for EditText fields so the system shows the correct keyboard and enforces basic input constraints. Finally, you will learn to avoid hardcoded strings by using string resources, and to set contentDescription for images to support accessibility. These skills matter because incorrect ids or missing attributes commonly cause crashes or poor user experiences. The hands-on login screen will combine these ideas: ids for username and password fields, hints for user guidance, inputType settings for name and password, and a button wired to Kotlin. screens.title: TextView — display text correctly
screens.subtitle: Attributes that control content, style, and localization

narration.text: A TextView displays text to the user. It’s simple but essential: labels, titles, and small dynamic messages all use TextView. In XML you typically set android:id to reference it from code, android:text for the initial content, android:textSize and android:textColor for presentation, and android:textStyle for bold or italic emphasis. A common beginner mistake is hardcoding display strings in android:text. Instead, define your strings in res/values/strings. xml and reference them with @string/your_string so your app can be localized and maintained easily. Another useful attribute is android:padding to create spacing inside the TextView. If you expect content to change at runtime, choose wrap_content for layout size so the view can expand naturally. Concrete example: a greeting TextView might start with "Hello, Android!" in XML but the app should replace that text at runtime with the user’s name. Misconception: TextView is only for static labels. In fact it frequently displays dynamic status, formatted text, and small clickable spans. Key takeaway: prefer string resources and meaningful ids, and set style attributes to make the text readable on different devices. Try swapping a hardcoded text for a string resource to see how localization-ready apps are built.

keyIdea.title: TextView in one line
keyIdea.text: Use TextView for readable text, prefer string resources to hardcoded text, and set size, color, and padding for clarity.

content.html:
Definition
TextView — display text correctly
Use attributes and string resources to control content and appearance.
XML example
<TextView
    android:id="@+id/greetingTextView"
    android:layout_width="wrap_content"
    android:layout_height="wrap_content"
    android:text="@string/hello_android"
    android:textSize="24sp"
    android:textColor="#FF0000"
    android:textStyle="bold|italic"
    android:padding="8dp" />
Explanation
  • android:id makes the view accessible from Kotlin with findViewById.
  • Use @string resources for text to support localization and maintenance.
  • textSize and textStyle control visual hierarchy and readability.
Example
Start with a greeting and replace the text at runtime with the user’s name to show personalization.
Key Takeaway

Prefer string resources for android:text, give a clear id, and choose readable size and color for accessibility.

Common mistake

Hardcoding text directly in XML. This prevents localization and increases maintenance cost.

Pro tip

Use wrap_content for a TextView that will change content, and consider maxLines if you want to clamp long messages.

Quick check

Can you replace a hardcoded android:text with a string resource and reference it in XML? That change improves localization readiness.

screens.title: Button — trigger actions from taps
screens.subtitle: Appearance attributes and preparing for click handling

narration.text: Buttons let users initiate actions such as submitting a form, navigating, or running validation. In XML, set android:id and android:text so the button can be found and labeled. You can tint the background using android:backgroundTint and control text color with android:textColor. These visual choices help buttons stand out and match your app theme. The real behavior comes from Kotlin: attach an OnClickListener to the button reference to perform work when the user taps. A common misconception is that Button attributes alone implement behavior; they only control the look. Another frequent mistake is forgetting android:id, which prevents code from finding the button and leads to null reference crashes. Concrete example: add a loginButton with text "Log In" and then in Kotlin read username and password EditText values when the button is tapped. When wiring clicks, remember to validate inputs before proceeding. Key takeaway: style buttons for visibility, give meaningful ids, and handle clicks in Kotlin with input validation. Practicing this pattern on the login screen teaches both the XML and the small but crucial Kotlin interaction. Button — trigger actions from taps means buttons are visual triggers — style them, give an id, and attach an onclicklistener in kotlin to perform actions.. In practical terms, appearance attributes and preparing for click handling. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Button behavior
keyIdea.text: Buttons are visual triggers — style them, give an id, and attach an OnClickListener in Kotlin to perform actions.

content.html:
Definition
Button — trigger actions from taps
Buttons need ids, labels, and a connected click listener to become interactive.
XML example
<Button
    android:id="@+id/loginButton"
    android:layout_width="match_parent"
    android:layout_height="wrap_content"
    android:text="Log In"
    android:backgroundTint="#6200EE"
    android:textColor="@android:color/white"
    android:layout_marginTop="16dp" />
Explanation
  • android:id allows findViewById to locate the button in Kotlin.
  • android:backgroundTint controls button color; match it to your theme for cohesion.
  • Always validate user input when the button triggers a form submission.
Example scenario
When the login button is tapped, read the username and password EditText values, check they are not empty, and then show an authenticated state or an error message.
Common mistake

Forgetting android:id or mis-typing the id. This causes findViewById to return null and may crash the app at runtime.

Check your understanding
Describe how you would validate the username field before proceeding after the button is pressed.

screens.title: ImageView — display images responsibly
screens.subtitle: src, scaleType, and accessibility with contentDescription

narration.text: ImageView displays images from drawable resources, the device, or the web, but in this chapter we focus on drawables shipped with your app. The key XML attributes are android:src to set the image resource, android:scaleType to control how the image fills the view bounds, and android:contentDescription for accessibility. Common scaleType values include centerCrop, fitCenter, and center, each affecting how the image is scaled and cropped. Always include contentDescription so screen readers can describe the image; if the image is purely decorative, use an empty contentDescription to skip it. A frequent misconception is that scaleType can fix any image aspect automatically; you still need to choose a view size that makes sense or use centerCrop to fill a fixed square while cropping excess. Concrete example: a 120dp profile ImageView with android:scaleType="centerCrop" will keep the image aspect while filling the square and cropping edges. If you forget contentDescription, users relying on assistive technology will miss critical context. Key takeaway: set src and scaleType for correct display and always provide contentDescription for accessibility. ImageView — display images responsibly means use android:src and android:scaletype to control display, and always include contentdescription for accessibility.. In practical terms, src, scaletype, and accessibility with contentdescription. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: ImageView essentials
keyIdea.text: Use android:src and android:scaleType to control display, and always include contentDescription for accessibility.

content.html:
Definition
ImageView — display images responsibly
Choose src and scaleType to control image fitting, and include contentDescription for screen readers.
XML example
<ImageView
    android:id="@+id/profileImageView"
    android:layout_width="120dp"
    android:layout_height="120dp"
    android:src="@drawable/ic_launcher_foreground"
    android:scaleType="centerCrop"
    android:contentDescription="User profile picture" />
Explanation
  • android:src points to drawable resources bundled with the app.
  • android:scaleType controls cropping and scaling; pick one that preserves important image content.
  • android:contentDescription is vital for accessibility and should describe the image purpose.
Example
A circular avatar often uses centerCrop to fill the shape while keeping the face centered. If the avatar is purely decorative, set contentDescription="" to avoid cluttering screen reader output.
Common mistake

Omitting contentDescription or using the wrong scaleType so important parts of the image are cropped out on different screens.

Pro tip
Choose scaleType to match your layout intent: centerCrop for filled squares, fitCenter for complete fit, and center for no scaling.

screens.title: EditText — collect user input correctly
screens.subtitle: hint, inputType, lines, and keyboard behavior

narration.text: EditText is a specialized TextView that accepts user input. The most important attributes to configure are android:hint, android:inputType, android:minLines/maxLines, and width/height. The hint guides users with placeholder text when the field is empty, while inputType tells the system what kind of data you expect and selects a matching keyboard layout. For example, inputType="number" presents a numeric keyboard and helps prevent non-numeric input; inputType="textPersonName" tailors suggestions for names; inputType="textPassword" hides characters for sensitive input. A common mistake is leaving inputType as the default, which may show the wrong keyboard and frustrate users. Also ensure EditText has a clear id so Kotlin can find it and read its text. Consider minLines and maxLines for multi-line fields. Concrete example: a username EditText uses hint="Username" and inputType="textPersonName" while a password field uses inputType="textPassword". Key takeaway: matching hint and inputType to the expected input reduces errors and improves the user's typing experience. EditText — collect user input correctly means set hint and inputtype to guide users and bring up the correct keyboard for the expected data.. In practical terms, hint, inputtype, lines, and keyboard behavior. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: EditText essentials
keyIdea.text: Set hint and inputType to guide users and bring up the correct keyboard for the expected data.

content.html:
Definition
EditText — collect user input correctly
Hints and inputType align user expectations with the keyboard and behavior you want.
XML example
<EditText
    android:id="@+id/nameEditText"
    android:layout_width="match_parent"
    android:layout_height="wrap_content"
    android:hint="Enter your name"
    android:inputType="textPersonName"
    android:minLines="1"
    android:maxLines="1"
    android:padding="12dp" />
Explanation
  • android:hint provides placeholder guidance when the field is empty.
  • android:inputType selects the keyboard and helps constrain input format.
  • Use minLines and maxLines to control the field height for multi-line entry.
Example
For an age field, set inputType to number so the numeric keypad appears. For email, use textEmailAddress so the keyboard offers the at-sign and email-friendly layout.
Common mistake

Using the wrong inputType, which leads to the wrong keyboard and more typing friction for users.

Try this
Change an EditText inputType to number and notice the different on-screen keyboard when you run the app on a device or emulator.

screens.title: Access views from Kotlin with findViewById
screens.subtitle: How to obtain references and update properties safely

narration.text: findViewById is the most direct way to access views from your Activity or Fragment. It matches the android:id you set in XML and returns a typed reference. To use it, call findViewById and provide the generated R. id identifier and the Kotlin view type so the returned value is correctly typed. After you have a reference, you can change text, colors, or visibility and attach listeners. A common pitfall is calling findViewById before setContentView, which returns null and leads to runtime errors. Another is mis-typing the id or using the wrong view type; both cause compile or runtime failures. Concrete example: in onCreate of MainActivity, call setContentView(R. layout. activity_main) and then val greetingTextView: TextView = findViewById(R. id. greetingTextView). After that you can set greetingTextView. text = "Welcome, User!" and change its color with setTextColor. When working with multiple views, name ids clearly and check they match XML exactly. While view binding provides safer access for larger projects, findViewById remains an essential concept for understanding how the code links to XML. Access views from Kotlin with findViewById means call setcontentview first, then use findviewbyid with the correct view type to manipulate ui elements safely.. In practical terms, how to obtain references and update properties safely. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: findViewById pattern
keyIdea.text: Call setContentView first, then use findViewById with the correct view type to manipulate UI elements safely.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough
Access views from Kotlin with findViewById
Call setContentView, then locate views by id and type to read or modify their properties.
Kotlin example
class MainActivity : AppCompatActivity() {
  override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
    super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)
    setContentView(R.layout.activity_main)

    // Find the TextView by its ID
    val greetingTextView: TextView = findViewById(R.id.greetingTextView)

    // Modify its properties
    greetingTextView.text = "Welcome, User!"
    greetingTextView.setTextColor(ContextCompat.getColor(this, R.color.purple_200))

    // Find the EditText for later reading
    val nameEditText: EditText = findViewById(R.id.nameEditText)
  }
}
Explanation
  • Always call setContentView before findViewById so the view hierarchy is available.
  • Use the correct Kotlin view type to get compile-time safety and clearer code.
  • After finding views, update text, colors, or attach listeners as needed.
Pitfall
Calling findViewById before setContentView or mis-typed ids returns null and often crashes the app with a NullPointerException.
Key Takeaway

Set content view, then find views by id with the correct type. This is the foundation for wiring UI to behavior.

screens.title: Build the Login Screen — XML starter template
screens.subtitle: A step-by-step layout using LinearLayout and core views

narration.text: Follow these steps to create the simple login screen from the hands-on activity. Start by creating activity_main. xml with a vertical LinearLayout root. Add padding to the root to keep content away from the edges. Step two: add a TextView for the title, style it larger and bold, and give it an id if you intend to change it from code. Step three: add an EditText for username with id usernameEditText, hint Username and inputType textPersonName. Step four: add an EditText for password with id passwordEditText, hint Password and inputType textPassword. Step five: add a Button with id loginButton and text Log In. Step six: add an ImageView at the bottom for a logo using android:src="@drawable/ic_launcher_foreground" and set an appropriate scaleType. Verify layout_width values are match_parent for inputs and button and wrap_content for the title and image as appropriate. This process ensures you have clear ids to access in Kotlin, correct hints and input types for user guidance, and a consistent arrangement. After building the XML, you will wire the login button to read EditText values in Kotlin. Build the Login Screen — XML starter template means create a vertical linearlayout, add title textview, two edittext fields with proper inputtype, a button, and a footer imageview with src.. In practical terms, a step-by-step layout using linearlayout and core views. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Login layout process
keyIdea.text: Create a vertical LinearLayout, add title TextView, two EditText fields with proper inputType, a Button, and a footer ImageView with src.

content.html:
Process Flow
Build the Login Screen — XML starter template
Follow a clear sequence to add title, inputs, button, and logo to a vertical LinearLayout.
Starter XML
<LinearLayout
    xmlns:android="http://schemas.android.com/apk/res/android"
    android:layout_width="match_parent"
    android:layout_height="match_parent"
    android:orientation="vertical"
    android:gravity="center_horizontal"
    android:padding="24dp"
    >

    <TextView
        android:id="@+id/titleTextView"
        android:layout_width="wrap_content"
        android:layout_height="wrap_content"
        android:text="Login"
        android:textSize="24sp"
        android:textStyle="bold" />

    <EditText
        android:id="@+id/usernameEditText"
        android:layout_width="match_parent"
        android:layout_height="wrap_content"
        android:hint="Username"
        android:inputType="textPersonName"
        android:layout_marginTop="16dp" />

    <EditText
        android:id="@+id/passwordEditText"
        android:layout_width="match_parent"
        android:layout_height="wrap_content"
        android:hint="Password"
        android:inputType="textPassword"
        android:layout_marginTop="8dp" />

    <Button
        android:id="@+id/loginButton"
        android:layout_width="match_parent"
        android:layout_height="wrap_content"
        android:text="Log In"
        android:layout_marginTop="16dp" />

    <ImageView
        android:id="@+id/logoImageView"
        android:layout_width="wrap_content"
        android:layout_height="wrap_content"
        android:src="@drawable/ic_launcher_foreground"
        android:contentDescription="App logo"
        android:layout_marginTop="24dp" />

</LinearLayout>
Step notes
  • Use match_parent for input widths so they fill the space for easier tapping.
  • Give clear ids so Kotlin code can find views by name.
  • Set hints and inputType so users know what to enter and get the proper keyboard.
Key Takeaway

Code Walkthrough
Wire the Login Button in Kotlin
Read input, validate, and respond with UI updates on button press.
Kotlin example
override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
  super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)
  setContentView(R.layout.activity_main)

  val usernameEditText: EditText = findViewById(R.id.usernameEditText)
  val passwordEditText: EditText = findViewById(R.id.passwordEditText)
  val loginButton: Button = findViewById(R.id.loginButton)
  val titleTextView: TextView = findViewById(R.id.titleTextView)

  loginButton.setOnClickListener {
    val username = usernameEditText.text.toString().trim()
    val password = passwordEditText.text.toString()

    if (username.isEmpty()) {
      titleTextView.text = "Please enter a username"
    } else {
      titleTextView.text = "Welcome, $username!"
    }
  }
}
Explanation
  • Convert EditText.text to a string before validation with toString().
  • Trim whitespace to avoid accidental empty values that look non-empty.
  • Use simple checks to guide the user before proceeding to authentication logic.
Common mistake
Assuming EditText.text is already a string or ignoring trimming, which can allow only-space names to pass validation.
Key Takeaway

Read EditText values as strings, validate, then update TextView or proceed. This small pattern is the heart of user-driven interactions.

screens.title: Common mistakes and fixes
screens.subtitle: Hardcoded text, missing ids, wrong inputType, and accessibility gaps

narration.text: Now that you can add views and wire interactions, let’s look at common mistakes and how to fix them. First, hardcoding strings with android:text blocks localization. Fix this by moving text into res/values/strings. xml and referencing it with @string/name. Second, forgetting android:id makes findViewById fail. Always assign clear ids that match your Kotlin code. Third, wrong inputType leads to poor keyboard choices; change inputType to number, textEmailAddress, or textPassword depending on the field. Fourth, missing contentDescription on ImageView prevents screen readers from conveying meaning; supply a descriptive text or an empty string for decorative images. Finally, calling findViewById before setContentView returns null; ensure you set the layout first in onCreate. Concrete example: if your age field uses inputType="text" instead of "number", users must switch keyboards and may type invalid characters. Fixing inputType reduces errors. Key takeaway: small XML mistakes are the common source of runtime issues and poor UX. Use the checklist: string resources, ids, inputType, contentDescription, and setContentView order to prevent them. In practical terms, hardcoded text, missing ids, wrong inputtype, and accessibility gaps. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. Comparison
Common mistakes and fixes
Small XML or ordering errors cause crashes or bad UX; compare mistake vs fix.
Mistake: Hardcoded text
android:text="Login" in XML is convenient but prevents localization.
Fix: Move to res/values/strings.xml and use @string/login_label.
Mistake: Missing id
No android:id means you cannot find the view in Kotlin and may crash when referencing it.
Fix: Add android:id="@+id/yourViewId" and match it in findViewById.
Mistake: Wrong inputType
Using text for numbers forces the user to switch keyboards and allows invalid characters.
Fix: Use inputType="number" for numeric fields to show the numeric keyboard and reduce errors.
Mistake: Missing contentDescription
Images without descriptions are invisible to assistive tech.
Fix: Provide android:contentDescription with useful text, or empty string for decorative images.

Use the five-item checklist to prevent the common mistakes that lead to crashes or poor UX.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: Three core concepts to carry forward

narration.text: These three core concepts capture the practical heart of the chapter. First, use string resources and clear android:id attributes in XML so your UI is localizable and accessible from Kotlin. Second, select the right attributes for each view: textSize and textStyle for TextView, backgroundTint and textColor for Button, src and scaleType for ImageView, and hint plus inputType for EditText. These attributes control look and usability. Third, connect layout and code reliably: call setContentView, then findViewById with the correct view type, read values from EditText as strings, validate input, and update TextView or other views in response to button taps. Practice the login screen to reinforce these ideas and use the checklist to catch common mistakes. Remember that small XML choices drive large differences in user experience, accessibility, and runtime behavior.
